The neonates of the Mottled rock rattlesnake (Crotalus lepidus) exhibit a snout-vent length of 20.4 centimeters [Lb = 20.4 centimeters] at birth, a value derived from field-captured gravid females that gave birth under controlled laboratory conditions. This modest size at emergence is typical for a species occupying the cooler, higher-elevation habitats of the Chihuahuan Desert, where thermal constraints likely influence early developmental rates. Field records indicate that the age at birth is approximately 122 days [ab = approximately 122 days], a gestation period determined by maintaining gravid females at a constant incubation temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] throughout pregnancy. This relatively protracted developmental phase contrasts with the shorter gestation lengths observed in several lowland congeners, suggesting an adaptive response to the reduced metabolic rates imposed by cooler environmental temperatures. The wet weight of a newly emerged hatchling averages 6.8 grams [Wwb = 6.8 grams], a value reflecting the substantial yolk reserves required to sustain the neonate through its first weeks of independent life before it begins exogenous feeding on small lizards and arthropods.

As female Crotalus lepidus progress through their juvenile phase, they undergo a predictable pattern of somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. The snout-vent length at which puberty is reached has been estimated at 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters] based on dissections of preserved museum specimens that were examined for the presence of developing ovarian follicles or enlarged testes. This threshold size, approximately double the length at birth, signifies the point at which gonadal activation begins, though successful copulation and fertilization may be deferred until a slightly larger body size is achieved. The typical reproductive output of this species consists of a single litter produced each year, with females giving birth to between 2 and 6 young per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 6 young per litter]. This low annual fecundity, combined with the production of just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], is consistent with the life-history strategy of a slow-living, capital-breeding viperid that relies on stored energy reserves accumulated over the active season to fuel gestation. The maximum reproductive rate expressed under optimal thermal conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] underscores the species' constrained reproductive potential relative to more fecund squamates.

Among adult females, the ultimate snout-vent length reaches a maximum of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], a figure obtained from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the Franklin Mountains of western Texas. This asymptotic body size is relatively modest for a crotaline snake of its genus, reflecting the energetic trade-offs imposed by the species' montane environment, where prey availability is seasonally pulsed and metabolic demands are elevated by frequent thermoregulatory basking. In conjunction with this ultimate length, the ultimate wet weight attained by large, reproductively active females has been recorded at 219 grams [Wwi = 219 grams], a mass that represents the upper bound of the species' body condition under natural foraging conditions. This weight is typically achieved only after several years of growth, as females allocate considerable resources to both somatic maintenance and the production of large, yolk-rich litters. The roughly 32-fold increase from the 6.8-gram neonate (6.8 grams) [Wwb = 6.8 grams] to the 219-gram adult female (219 grams) [Wwi = 219 grams] illustrates a body mass trajectory that demands efficient energy assimilation throughout the active foraging season.

The physiological longevity of Crotalus lepidus has been documented through captive-maintenance studies and field recapture data, revealing a maximum lifespan of approximately 33.6 years [am = approximately 33.6 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This remarkably extended lifespan, one of the longest recorded among North American pitvipers, positions the Mottled rock rattlesnake as an extreme example of a slow life-history strategy within its clade. The species' ability to persist for over three decades likely stems from its low extrinsic mortality rate in the wild, combined with a conservative metabolic strategy that minimizes oxidative damage over time. Comparative analyses with related species such as Crotalus atrox and Crotalus viridis suggest that the elevated longevity of C. lepidus may be linked to its occupation of cooler, less productive habitats where the pace of life is intrinsically slower. The 33.6-year figure (approximately 33.6 years) [am = approximately 33.6 years] represents an upper bound under predator-free, controlled conditions, and field-based estimates of maximum observed longevity are typically somewhat lower, though still notable for a reptile of this body size at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

The reproductive strategy of Crotalus lepidus is tightly coupled to its slow growth and extended lifespan, with females typically deferring their first reproductive event until they have achieved a body size that can support the high energetic demands of gestation. Under field conditions, females initiating their first litter produce between 2 and 6 young per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 6 young per litter], and a single litter is produced each year [F_R_i = single litter is produced each year], a schedule that is consistent across most of the species' range. The maximum reproductive rate of the species, expressed as 3.6 young per year [Ri = 3.6 young per year], is achieved only when environmental conditions are optimal and when the female has reached her ultimate body size of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters] and a mass of 219 grams [Wwi = 219 grams]. This annual output represents the product of a modest litter size and a low reproductive frequency, reinforcing the species' position as a classic K-selected organism. The long interval between successive litters, combined with a 122-day gestation period (122 days) [ab = 122 days] at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], means that females can produce only a limited number of offspring over their exceptionally long lives.
